(CNN) -- Madagascar's military handed over the reins of the island nation to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina on Wednesday, ending a two-month long political crisis -- but apparently creating a constitutional one. Andry Rajoelina is six years too young to be Madagascar's president under its constitution. Rajoelina, a former disc jockey turned mayor of Madagascar's capital, declared himself president of a transitional government and his supporters pledged to hold elections in two years. But Rajoelina, at 34, is six years too young to be president, according to the country's constitution. Also, the constitution says the head of parliament's upper house must call elections within two months if something happens to the president. Madagascar's former president, Marc Ravalomanana, ceded power to his military Tuesday after insisting over the weekend that he would remain in control. Analysts think Ravalomanana had little choice but to step down once he had lost much of the army's support. The African Union had warned that any power transfer aided by the military would amount to a coup d' etat. The Union has since removed any mention of a coup in its official communique and called on the transitional government to "comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements." Monja Roindefo, the opposition-appointed prime minister, vigorously defended the week's developments on the island, located off the southeastern coast of Africa. "Well, we would like to define what is a coup," he told CNN on Wednesday. "A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn't work anymore." "As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa," he added. Roindefo said the new government will hold elections but has given itself two years to clean up the process.  Watch more from iReporters and Twitterers on the crisis » . "How could you make an election immediately?" he said. "We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country." The African Union also asked that all steps be taken to ensure the safety of the former president. The opposition leader had called for Ravalomanana's arrest, accusing him of corruption, financial mismanagement and dictatorship. Ravalomanana was first elected in 2001 and won a second term in 2006. To many Malagasy, he represented a new breed of politician -- a self-made millionaire, a no-nonsense business leader. But Ravalomanana maintained his business empire while in office and it was unclear to many where his business interests ended and his political leadership began. His recent purchase of a $60 million airplane further stoked public discontent. Opposition leader Rajoelina was quick to seize on the sentiments and made fiery appeals to the country's impoverished masses. The country was plunged into political instability in January after thousands of people took to the streets to protest rising food prices and what they perceived as autocratic behavior by Ravalomanana. The protests soon degenerated into rioting and looting, and left about 100 people dead.  Watch more on president's resignation » . Soon after, Rajoelina declared that he was in charge of the country. He gave Ravalomanana until early February to step down. The president responded by firing Rajoelina as mayor of the capital, inciting the latter's supporters to once again descend on the streets. More deadly violence followed. Clashes spread to most provincial capitals and other cities across the country, with homes and businesses looted and burned, the U.S. State Department reported. CNN's David McKenzie contributed to this report.

Under the nation's constitution, Rajoelina falls six years short of the minimum age required to serve as president.

Rajoelina, a former disc jockey who rose to become mayor of Madagascar's capital, declared himself head of a transitional government, with his supporters pledging to hold elections within two years. However, at 34, Rajoelina does not meet the constitutional age requirement for the presidency. Furthermore, the constitution stipulates that the head of parliament's upper house must call elections within two months should the presidency become vacant.

Madagascar's former president, Marc Ravalomanana, relinquished power to the military on Tuesday, reversing his earlier insistence over the weekend that he would remain in control. Analysts suggest that Ravalomanana had little recourse but to step down once he had lost the bulk of the army's backing.

The African Union had previously cautioned that any military-assisted transfer of power would constitute a coup d'état. Since then, however, the Union has withdrawn any reference to a coup from its official communiqué, instead calling on the transitional government to "comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements."

Monja Roindefo, the prime minister appointed by the opposition, staunchly defended the week's events on the island nation, located off Africa's southeastern coast. "Well, we would like to define what is a coup," he told CNN on Wednesday. "A coup is when a group of people seizes power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when representative democracy no longer functions." He added, "As stated in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend themselves against oppression or dictatorship in Africa."

Roindefo indicated that the new government intends to hold elections, but has allotted itself two years to reform the process. "How could you hold an election immediately?" he asked. "We need to reform the electoral commission. ... The 24 months we have given ourselves will be used to prepare for these elections, in order to build a genuinely democratic nation."

The African Union also called for measures to ensure the safety of the former president, whom the opposition leader had sought to have arrested on charges of corruption, financial mismanagement, and dictatorial conduct.

Ravalomanana was first elected in 2001 and secured a second term in 2006. In response, the president dismissed Rajoelina from his post as mayor of the capital, reigniting protests among his supporters and triggering further deadly violence. The unrest spread to most provincial capitals and other cities across the country, with homes and businesses looted and burned, according to the U.S. State Department.

# Madagascar's Political Crisis Resolves as Military Hands Power to Rajoelina

Madagascar's two-month political crisis reached a pivotal turning point on Wednesday when the military formally transferred power to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina. While the transfer brought an end to weeks of turmoil and uncertainty, it simultaneously opened the door to fresh constitutional and legal questions that could shape the island nation's political future.

## A Young Leader Facing Constitutional Hurdles

At the center of this transition is Rajoelina, a 34-year-old former disc jockey who rose to prominence as mayor of the capital city before emerging as the figurehead of the opposition movement. His ascent to power, however, is complicated by a significant legal obstacle: Madagascar's constitution stipulates that presidents must be at least 40 years old. This six-year gap between Rajoelina's age and the constitutional requirement has raised serious questions about the legitimacy and durability of the new arrangement, leaving observers to wonder how—or whether—this discrepancy will be addressed.

## The Fall of Ravalomanana

The power transfer followed the dramatic unraveling of former President Marc Ravalomanana's authority. Despite his earlier public declarations that he would retain control of the government no matter the pressure, Ravalomanana's position became untenable as he steadily lost the backing of much of the armed forces. Recognizing that his hold on power was no longer sustainable without military support, he ultimately ceded control to the armed forces, paving the way for the handover to Rajoelina's opposition movement.

## International Reaction: From Coup Warnings to Cautious Engagement

The African Union's response to these developments reflected the delicate diplomatic balancing act facing regional bodies confronting unconstitutional transfers of power. Initially, the AU issued a stark warning that any transfer of power facilitated by military intervention would be classified as a coup d'état—a designation carrying significant diplomatic and economic consequences. However, in a notable softening of its stance, the organization later withdrew this characterization from its official language. Instead of branding the transition a coup, the AU shifted its approach to urging Madagascar's transitional government to adhere to constitutional procedures moving forward, suggesting a more pragmatic engagement with the new political reality on the ground.

## The Government's Defense: Democracy, Not a Coup

Newly appointed Prime Minister Monja Roindefo, installed by the opposition, has firmly rejected characterizations of the transition as a coup. In his defense of the new government's legitimacy, Roindefo framed the events not as an unconstitutional seizure of power but as a necessary corrective measure in response to what he described as a failure of representative democracy under the previous administration. He emphasized that the transitional arrangement was intended to be temporary, with plans in place to hold elections within a two-year timeframe—a commitment aimed at reassuring both domestic and international observers that the current arrangement represents a bridge to restored constitutional governance rather than a permanent departure from democratic norms.

## Looking Ahead

As Madagascar moves forward under this new transitional leadership, the coming months will likely test whether Rajoelina's government can navigate the constitutional challenges surrounding his age, maintain the fragile support of the military, and fulfill promises of a return to electoral democracy—all while managing the complex diplomatic relationships with international bodies like the African Union that remain watchful of how the situation unfolds.

# Madagascar's 2009 Political Crisis: Ravalomanana's Resignation and Rajoelina's Rise

## Background
Marc Ravalomanana had served as President of Madagascar since 2002. By late 2008 and early 2009, his government faced growing public discontent over economic issues, allegations of authoritarian governance, and controversial deals (including a land lease agreement with a South Korean company that sparked public outrage).

## The Rise of Andry Rajoelina
Andry Rajoelina, the young mayor of Antananarivo (the capital), emerged as the leader of the opposition movement. Tensions escalated when:
- The government shut down Rajoelina's television station
- Rajoelina was removed from his position as mayor
- Rajoelina declared himself the head of a transitional authority, positioning himself as an alternative leader

## Escalation of the Crisis
The situation deteriorated through early 2009:
- Mass protests occurred in Antananarivo
- Security forces opened fire on demonstrators near the presidential palace, killing dozens of protesters
- Segments of the military eventually withdrew support from Ravalomanana and sided with opposition forces
- Rajoelina's supporters occupied key government buildings

## Ravalomanana's Resignation and Power Transfer
In March 2009, facing military pressure and loss of control, Ravalomanana resigned. However, the manner of the transition raised significant constitutional concerns:

- **Constitutional bypass**: Rather than following the constitutional line of succession (which would have designated the Senate president or another official as interim leader), Ravalomanana reportedly transferred power directly to a military directorate
- **Military role**: The military then handed power to Rajoelina, effectively installing him as President of the High Transitional Authority
- **Legality disputed**: This transfer was widely characterized as a coup d'état, since Rajoelina assumed power outside normal constitutional processes, and he was significantly below the minimum age required by Madagascar's constitution to serve as president

## International Response
The transfer of power was condemned by:
- The African Union, which suspended Madagascar's membership
- The Southern African Development Community (SADC)
- Various international bodies that refused to recognize Rajoelina's government as legitimate, characterizing it as unconstitutional

## Aftermath
Madagascar entered a period of political isolation and instability, with Rajoelina heading a transitional government. This crisis ultimately led to years of negotiations, mediation attempts, and eventually elections in 2013 aimed at restoring constitutional order, in which neither Ravalomanana nor Rajoelina were candidates due to negotiated agreements.

# Madagascar's 2009 Crisis: How a Political Standoff Became a Military-Backed Takeover

**ANTANANARIVO** — In early 2009, Madagascar descended into one of the most significant political upheavals in its post-colonial history, culminating in the ouster of President Marc Ravalomanana and the installation of opposition leader Andry Rajoelina, then the young mayor of the capital, Antananarivo. The crisis, which unfolded over several tense weeks, exposed deep fractures in the island nation's democratic institutions and raised troubling questions about the military's role in mediating political disputes.

## Roots of the Discontent

The unrest did not emerge in a vacuum. For months prior to the crisis, grievances had been building against Ravalomanana's government, which critics accused of authoritarian tendencies, economic mismanagement, and self-dealing. Chief among the controversies was a land deal involving the South Korean firm Daewoo Logistics, which sought a long-term lease on vast swaths of Malagasy farmland—an arrangement many Malagasy viewed as a sellout of national resources to foreign interests.

Rajoelina, then just 34 years old, capitalized on this discontent. As mayor of the capital, he began holding mass rallies that drew tens of thousands of supporters, positioning himself as a voice for ordinary Malagasy people against what he characterized as an increasingly out-of-touch and self-enriching presidency.

Tensions escalated dramatically when Ravalomanana's government shut down Rajoelina's television station, Viva TV, accusing it of inciting unrest. The move backfired, transforming Rajoelina from a regional political figure into a national symbol of resistance.

## Violence and the Military's Pivotal Role

The crisis turned deadly in late January 2009, when security forces opened fire on demonstrators near the presidential palace, killing dozens of protesters. The bloodshed hardened opposition sentiment and accelerated calls for Ravalomanana's removal.

What followed was a gradual but decisive shift in military allegiance. Rather than suppressing the opposition movement, significant factions within Madagascar's armed forces began withdrawing support from Ravalomanana. By March, this defection had become impossible to ignore: soldiers occupied key government buildings, including the presidential palace, effectively transferring control to Rajoelina's opposition movement.

Military officials who backed the transition framed their actions not as a coup but as an intervention necessary to prevent further bloodshed and restore order. This narrative—positioning the armed forces as reluctant arbiters rather than active plotters—became central to how the transition was subsequently described by its architects, even as international observers largely characterized it as an unconstitutional seizure of power.

## The Opposition's Justification

Rajoelina and his supporters constructed a justification for the takeover built on several pillars. They argued that Ravalomanana had violated democratic norms through increasing consolidation of power, pointing to his control over key media outlets and allegations of using state resources for personal business interests. The Daewoo land deal, in particular, was repeatedly invoked as evidence that the president had betrayed national sovereignty for personal or political gain.

The opposition also leaned heavily on the deaths of protesters as moral justification, framing the transition as a necessary response to a government that had turned violent against its own citizens. This narrative of popular uprising against an illegitimate, increasingly autocratic leader allowed Rajoelina's movement to present the transfer of power as a democratic correction rather than an unconstitutional rupture—despite the transition occurring through military pressure rather than electoral or constitutional processes.

## International Isolation and Domestic Consequences

The international response was swift and largely unified in its condemnation. The African Union suspended Madagascar's membership, characterizing the transition as an unconstitutional change of government. The United States, the European Union, and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) similarly refused to recognize Rajoelina's government as legitimate, and international donors—upon whom Madagascar's economy heavily depended—suspended significant aid packages.

This isolation proved economically devastating for a country already among the world's poorest. Foreign investment stalled, tourism revenue collapsed, and the suspension of donor aid crippled public services in a nation where a substantial portion of the government budget relied on international assistance.

Domestically, the political transition did little to resolve the underlying instability. Rajoelina's High Transitional Authority struggled to establish legitimacy, facing continued opposition from Ravalomanana loyalists and skepticism from segments of the population who viewed the change in power as merely replacing one set of elites with another.

## A Fragile Aftermath

The crisis ultimately prolonged Madagascar's political uncertainty for years. Promised elections were repeatedly delayed, and the transitional government's inability to secure international recognition contributed to a broader economic malaise that deepened poverty across the island nation. It was not until 2013 that elections—notably excluding both Ravalomanana and Rajoelina as candidates, per a negotiated agreement—began to restore some semblance of constitutional order.

The 2009 crisis remains a cautionary case study in how popular grievances, media suppression, and military defection can combine to topple a government through means that occupy an ambiguous space between popular uprising and coup d'état—a distinction that continues to shape debates about Madagascar's fragile democratic institutions today.
